title: 'Pati Patni Aur Woh Do' Opens Soft at ₹24 Crore — Is Ayushmann Khurrana's Everyman Formula Running Out of Road?
excerpt: The Bollywood sequel managed weekend growth but its ₹1.82 crore overseas haul signals diaspora audiences had other plans
body:
Ayushmann Khurrana has built a career on being Bollywood's reliable middle-class hero — the guy who picks scripts no one else would touch and turns them into sleeper hits. But *Pati Patni Aur Woh Do*, the sequel to the 2019 romantic comedy, is testing the limits of that formula.

The film opened on May 15 to ₹3.85 crore nett in India — Ayushmann's lowest opening in recent memory, trailing even his modest *An Action Hero* debut of ₹1.31 crore only because of the sequel's wider release. By the end of its first weekend, the worldwide gross sat at ₹24.25 crore. That's not a disaster, but for a film banking on the Bollywood sequel playbook and a cast that includes Sara Ali Khan, it's a quiet thud.

## The Numbers Tell a Mixed Story

Day 1 brought ₹3.85 crore in India with tepid occupancy. Saturday improved to ₹5.75 crore — a 43.8% jump — suggesting some word-of-mouth was kicking in. Sunday pushed further to ₹7.75 crore domestically, bringing the India total to ₹17.35 crore and the worldwide figure to ₹24.25 crore.

Overseas earnings tell the harder truth: ₹1.82 crore across the first weekend, per Bollywood Hungama's tracking. For a Hindi comedy with recognizable faces, that's thin. The original *Pati Patni Aur Woh* (2019), which starred Kartik Aaryan, performed modestly overseas too — but it had the novelty factor. A sequel needs either a bigger hook or a louder marketing campaign, and this one had neither.

Sacnilk reported 6,822 shows on Day 1, a healthy screen count, but occupancy hovered around 22% by Sunday — meaning theatres were giving it room, but audiences weren't filling seats.

## What Went Wrong (and What Didn't)

The pre-release buzz was strikingly muted. Unlike the original, which benefited from Kartik Aaryan's then-rising star power and a marketable "infidelity comedy" hook, the sequel had to explain why it existed at all. Ayushmann himself clarified in interviews that the film avoids the infidelity angle — a creative choice that may have dulled the franchise's signature edge.

Director Mudassar Aziz, who helmed the original, returned for the sequel, but the promotional campaign never found a viral moment or a trailer scene that sparked debate. In a market where *Karuppu* was commanding screens and social media attention, *Pati Patni Aur Woh Do* struggled for oxygen.

What it did get right: Saturday and Sunday saw genuine growth, suggesting the film plays better than its marketing sold it. Audiences who showed up seem to be recommending it to friends — the classic "decent film, bad opening" pattern that has saved several Bollywood midrange films in recent years.

## The Diaspora View

For NRIs who grew up on Bollywood comedies, the franchise exists in a familiar sweet spot: light, watchable, and perfect for a weekend outing when nothing else is playing in Hindi. But at ₹1.82 crore overseas, many diaspora audiences clearly chose *Karuppu* or stayed home.

The sequel's problem in diaspora markets mirrors its domestic challenge: there was no conversation around it. In the US and UK, Hindi films increasingly need social-media-driven anticipation to pull NRI audiences into theatres. Without a meme, a controversy, or a trailer moment, the film was invisible in a crowded release calendar.

## The Monday Test

The coming weekdays will determine whether *Pati Patni Aur Woh Do* stabilises as a modest earner or slides further. Trade analysts peg the break-even at around ₹70 crore — a target that looks ambitious at the current pace, though not mathematically impossible if the film holds steady.

For Ayushmann, it's a reminder that even the most trusted brand needs reinvention. His next choices will matter more than this film's final number.
